currentContext.business: Jindal Stainless Limited manufactures and sells stainless-steel products; BRSR Section A records manufacturing of 'Metal & Metal Products' as 100% of turnover under NIC code 24105. The Company operates an integrated platform spanning melting, hot rolling, annealing and pickling, cold rolling, long products, ferro alloys and specialised downstream solutions, with manufacturing divisions at Hisar (Haryana), Jajpur (Odisha), Vizag and a Mobility Division at Pathredi, alongside overseas operations including an Indonesian melt shop and NPI smelter and a service centre in Spain. It sells to traders, OEMs, pipe and tube manufacturers, hollowware producers, automotive players, re-rollers, wagon and coach manufacturers, white-goods makers and lift/elevator/metro system providers across B2B, MSME (B2ECA), retail (B2C) and government (B2G) channels; exports were ~10% of turnover in FY 2025-26.

currentContext.expansion: JSL's FY26 expansion story has three legs: upstream melting in Indonesia, downstream rolling in India, and circularity/renewables. In March 2026 (Q4 FY26) it commissioned, ahead of schedule and through its joint-venture operations, the 1.2 MTPA stainless steel melt shop in Indonesia (PT Glory Metal Indonesia), lifting total melting capacity by over 40% to 4.2 MTPA including 3 MTPA in India; the facility sits near a region accounting for 70-75% of global nickel supply and will ship slabs to JSL's downstream units at Jajpur and Mundra. Downstream, the Company is commissioning a 1.1 MTPA Hot Rolled Annealed Pickled (HRAP) line and a 0.17 MTPA Cold Rolled Annealed Pickled (CRAP) line at Jajpur, Odisha by Q4 FY27 and Q2 FY27 respectively, as part of a previously announced INR 1,900 crore investment, and has committed a further INR 900 crore to cold rolling at Hisar and Kharagpur with commissioning planned by Q2 FY28 — together taking CRAP capacity from 2.05 MTPA in FY26 to 2.67 MTPA by FY28 and enabling thinner cold-rolled products. Longer term, a non-binding MoU signed in FY25 with the Government of Maharashtra explores an INR 40,000 crore investment over the next decade for a stainless steel manufacturing facility in the state. On circularity and energy, JSL initiated a new wet milling plant at Jajpur with Harsco Environmental to double slag processing capacity, under a USD 150 million, 15-year agreement; commissioned with AB Energia Solutions Odisha's largest captive industrial solar plant at Jajpur at over 30 MWp (7.324 MWp floating plus 23.02 MWp rooftop, ~44.3 million units a year, cutting CO2 by around 32,208 metric tonnes annually); and partnered Oyster Renewable Energy on a 315.6 MW solar-wind hybrid project in Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat at an investment of INR 132 crore by the Company, expected to abate around 6.5 lakh metric tonnes of carbon a year once fully operational. Its strategic arm Jindal Defense and Aerospace commissioned an electro slag remelting facility for high-performance alloys, and Jindal Stainless Steelway Limited is investing in a dedicated stainless steel fabrication plant after the infrastructure segment grew from a single 2021 project to 20+ executed projects with a pipeline across Indian Railways, state PWDs and municipal corporations. Raw-material backward integration continues through a chrome ore linkage with Odisha Mining Corporation, development of captive mining assets at Sukinda, 70-72% scrap-based inputs, and the 49% stake in the Indonesian NPI joint venture. The Directors' Report technology-absorption list shows a green hydrogen plant and a Zero Liquid Discharge plant imported in 2025-26 and still under commissioning.
currentContext.mdna: India is expected to remain the fastest-growing major stainless steel market and the world's second-largest, driven by infrastructure, construction, transportation, manufacturing and capital goods; the Company frames India as its primary focus market.|Headroom in per-capita consumption: India's per capita stainless steel consumption is ~3.6 kg against a global average of about 7 kg. ISSDA-reported domestic consumption rose to 5.16 MT in FY26 from 4.8 MT in FY25 (3.50 MT in FY20).|Global melt shop production is expected to rise from 64.16 MT in CY25 to 64.35 MT in CY26 and 65.76 MT in CY27 (+0.3% and +2.2% Y-O-Y), a stable broad-based recovery rather than a demand surge.|Policy tailwinds: PLI Scheme 1.2 for specialty steel (85 projects, 55 companies, INR 11,887 crore committed investment and ~8.7 million tonnes of capacity additions) and the Quality Control Order framework, expected to support capacity expansion, product diversification and value-added grades.|Import pressure is the principal margin headwind — low-priced and substandard imports, and global overcapacity and trade diversion into India from protectionism elsewhere, continue to pressure domestic pricing.|Trade policy is reshaping flows: the EU safeguard quota mechanism, CBAM introducing carbon-linked costs, and the US Section 232 steel tariff increase from 25% to 50% on June 4, 2025, redirecting exporters into alternative markets and raising competitive intensity.|Input volatility: nickel and chromium price movements directly influence production costs and margins; management positions integrated sourcing, flexible production and cleaner energy as the offset.|Fuel and industrial-gas availability was a late-FY26 constraint — limited availability of LPG, propane and natural gas led to rationalised plant utilisation, with a more pronounced impact on scrap-based producers than on integrated facilities; further clarity on fuel allocation would improve production planning.|Prices are expected to remain firm on elevated alloying-material input costs, though short-term movements may stay volatile with global commodity markets.|Sector demand is skewing to value-added and high-performance grades — aerospace, defence, renewable energy, electric mobility, food processing, chemicals and advanced engineering — with 300-series grades still the largest demand share.|Automotive demand: FY26 total vehicle production of ~34.7 million units and highest-ever sales of 46.43 lakh units (+7.9% Y-O-Y); two-wheelers and passenger vehicles account for nearly 85-90% of stainless steel consumption within the automotive segment, with safety, emission norms and lightweighting expected to raise stainless intensity per vehicle.|QCO timing is a live variable: finished stainless flat products were exempted from QCO compliance from April 2026, extended in June 2026 through March 31, 2027, with input-material QCO norms deferred to September 30, 2026.

risks.risk: Raw material price risk — nickel, ferrochrome and scrap
risks.note: Dependence on nickel, ferrochrome and scrap prices exposes the Company to global commodity price volatility and supply fluctuations, which can impact raw material costs and margins. Mitigated through diversified domestic and international sourcing, long-term supplier partnerships, a joint venture securing nickel pig iron, and a ferrochrome mix of scrap, captive mines and supplies from Odisha Mining Corporation.

risks.risk: Import risk — low-cost imports and pricing pressure
risks.note: Low-cost imports, especially from China and FTA-linked markets, create pricing pressure and affect domestic competitiveness. The response is new grades, expanded applications, support for BIS standards and Quality Control Orders, and portfolio diversification.

Geopolitical tensions, natural disasters and global disruptions may impact logistics and raw material availability; mitigated by a diversified supplier base, more domestic and regional sourcing, and flexible procurement.

Changes in environmental, product-quality and industry regulations may impact compliance requirements and operating costs. The Company monitors regulatory change, prepares for early compliance and participates in policy discussion including the proposed National Stainless Steel Policy.

risks.risk: Financial risk — interest rates and foreign exchange
risks.note: Exposure to interest rate fluctuations and foreign exchange volatility arising from import-export operations; managed through disciplined leverage, refinancing and maturity management, and hedging.

Increasing digitalisation raises exposure to cyber threats, data breaches and operational disruptions; addressed via cybersecurity systems, ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification, regular security audits, employee training and structured incident response.

Regulatory shifts such as CBAM and dependence on imported critical inputs like nickel increase climate-related risk. Mitigation runs through renewable energy, low-emission technologies, higher scrap usage, circular-economy practice, backward integration, stronger carbon accounting and evaluation of green hydrogen and electrification.

risks.risk: Occupational health and safety across a large, geographically dispersed workforce (BRSR material issue 8)
risks.note: With employees and contract workers across multiple plant locations, any significant safety incident or regulatory non-compliance can cause operational disruption, production losses, higher absenteeism and attrition, and reputational damage. Managed under a 'No Harm' / 'Zero Harm' philosophy with LTIFR and fatality monitoring, safety training, and Spirometry/Audiometry health surveillance in dust-prone and high-noise environments.

risks.risk: Human capital management — talent attraction and retention (BRSR material issue 7)
risks.note: Evolving workforce expectations, demand for flexible working and intensifying competition for skilled talent present a strategic risk to operational continuity, strategic execution and corporate reputation; addressed through inclusive policies, career development, engagement and capability-building.

guidance: revenue growth: 9-10% YoY maintained; margin: unchanged; order inflow: no specific guidance; capex/commissioning: FY26 capex guidance INR 2,700cr (H1 spent INR 1,260cr); NPI at 90%, Chromeni ramping to 80% in H2, SMS Indonesia early FY27, cold rolling end FY27, HRAP H2 FY27
segment / subsidiary detail: Flat products: 34% 200-series, 49% 300-series, 17% 400-series; long products: rebar sales rising (2,000-2,500 tons/month), wire rod moderating; fabrication: new Patalganga unit operational; exports: subdued due to CBAM uncertainty; NPI: EBITDA positive, $500-1,500/ton range; Chromeni: 70% utilization, targeting 80% in H2

risks & watch-items: QCO suspension until Dec 2025 enabling cheap imports; CBAM uncertainty delaying export recovery; global demand softness in US/EU; ferrochrome price volatility; land acquisition delays for Maharashtra plant; potential margin pressure from import competition
management quality / tone: Confident and disciplined; focused on execution, quality, and sustainability; cautious on guidance revisions due to external uncertainties; proactive on policy advocacy (QCO, PLI); optimistic on long-term infrastructure demand and green transition
non-obvious takeaways: 6,700 fabricators trained in Q2 (cumulative 60,400) — building ecosystem lock-in for stainless steel in infra; green hydrogen plant (600 NMQ/hr) is among India’s largest planned for steel; Sukinda mine (own chrome ore) to start FY27 — rare backward integration in Indian stainless steel

themes.title: Metals & mining cycle - steel, aluminium, critical minerals
themes.need: Domestic demand growth, safeguard duties and an India capacity-expansion wave lift integrated metals while critical-mineral security gains policy support. TATASTEEL targets 45-50 MT India (FY26 India EBITDA INR34,272cr at 24% margin) with a +INR6,000/t 1QFY27 realisation uplift; JINDALSTEL/SAIL/JSWSTEEL-tier on steel; HINDALCO/NALCO on aluminium; HINDZINC on zinc (Q1FY27 all-time-record EBITDA INR8,074cr +109% YoY on a record-low zinc cost-of-production USD851/t, though CEO Arun Misra hands over to ex-SAIL chief Amarendu Prakash 1-Aug-2026 and a new Gundlupet REE/Yttrium critical-minerals block won this quarter is a 2031-32-dated option, not near-term); NMDC/COALINDIA/LLOYDSME/SARDAEN on iron-ore/coal/integrated mining. Q1FY27 also quantified the export-side shock and the downstream escape from it: JINDALSAW's consolidated PAT fell 78% YoY to INR 91cr on +9% revenue because the Strait-of-Hormuz blockade suspended ALL India-origin MENA export shipments from March 2026, holding utilisation at ~60-65%; SHYAMMETL took the other route, posting INR 5,455cr revenue (+23.3%) at a multi-quarter-high 14.9% EBITDA margin with aluminium EBITDA/t +52% YoY and specialty alloys near 20.5% margin, self-funding ~INR 9,580cr of balance capex with no debt.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Jindal Stainless Limited manufactures and sells stainless-steel products; BRSR Section A records manufacturing of 'Metal & Metal Products' as 100% of turnover under NIC code 24105. The Company operates an integrated platform spanning melting, hot rolling, annealing and pickling, cold rolling, long products, ferro alloys and specialised downstream solutions, with manufacturing divisions at Hisar (Haryana), Jajpur (Odisha), Vizag and a Mobility Division at Pathredi, alongside overseas operations including an Indonesian melt shop and NPI smelter and a service centre in Spain. It sells to traders, OEMs, pipe and tube manufacturers, hollowware producers, automotive players, re-rollers, wagon and coach manufacturers, white-goods makers and lift/elevator/metro system providers across B2B, MSME (B2ECA), retail (B2C) and government (B2G) channels; exports were ~10% of turnover in FY 2025-26.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- India is expected to remain the fastest-growing major stainless steel market and the world's second-largest, driven by infrastructure, construction, transportation, manufacturing and capital goods; the Company frames India as its primary focus market.
- Headroom in per-capita consumption: India's per capita stainless steel consumption is ~3.6 kg against a global average of about 7 kg. ISSDA-reported domestic consumption rose to 5.16 MT in FY26 from 4.8 MT in FY25 (3.50 MT in FY20).
- Global melt shop production is expected to rise from 64.16 MT in CY25 to 64.35 MT in CY26 and 65.76 MT in CY27 (+0.3% and +2.2% Y-O-Y), a stable broad-based recovery rather than a demand surge.
- Policy tailwinds: PLI Scheme 1.2 for specialty steel (85 projects, 55 companies, INR 11,887 crore committed investment and ~8.7 million tonnes of capacity additions) and the Quality Control Order framework, expected to support capacity expansion, product diversification and value-added grades.
- Import pressure is the principal margin headwind — low-priced and substandard imports, and global overcapacity and trade diversion into India from protectionism elsewhere, continue to pressure domestic pricing.
- Trade policy is reshaping flows: the EU safeguard quota mechanism, CBAM introducing carbon-linked costs, and the US Section 232 steel tariff increase from 25% to 50% on June 4, 2025, redirecting exporters into alternative markets and raising competitive intensity.
- Input volatility: nickel and chromium price movements directly influence production costs and margins; management positions integrated sourcing, flexible production and cleaner energy as the offset.
- Fuel and industrial-gas availability was a late-FY26 constraint — limited availability of LPG, propane and natural gas led to rationalised plant utilisation, with a more pronounced impact on scrap-based producers than on integrated facilities; further clarity on fuel allocation would improve production planning.
- Prices are expected to remain firm on elevated alloying-material input costs, though short-term movements may stay volatile with global commodity markets.
- Sector demand is skewing to value-added and high-performance grades — aerospace, defence, renewable energy, electric mobility, food processing, chemicals and advanced engineering — with 300-series grades still the largest demand share.
- Automotive demand: FY26 total vehicle production of ~34.7 million units and highest-ever sales of 46.43 lakh units (+7.9% Y-O-Y); two-wheelers and passenger vehicles account for nearly 85-90% of stainless steel consumption within the automotive segment, with safety, emission norms and lightweighting expected to raise stainless intensity per vehicle.
- QCO timing is a live variable: finished stainless flat products were exempted from QCO compliance from April 2026, extended in June 2026 through March 31, 2027, with input-material QCO norms deferred to September 30, 2026.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: JSL's FY26 expansion story has three legs: upstream melting in Indonesia, downstream rolling in India, and circularity/renewables. In March 2026 (Q4 FY26) it commissioned, ahead of schedule and through its joint-venture operations, the 1.2 MTPA stainless steel melt shop in Indonesia (PT Glory Metal Indonesia), lifting total melting capacity by over 40% to 4.2 MTPA including 3 MTPA in India; the facility sits near a region accounting for 70-75% of global nickel supply and will ship slabs to JSL's downstream units at Jajpur and Mundra. Downstream, the Company is commissioning a 1.1 MTPA Hot Rolled Annealed Pickled (HRAP) line and a 0.17 MTPA Cold Rolled Annealed Pickled (CRAP) line at Jajpur, Odisha by Q4 FY27 and Q2 FY27 respectively, as part of a previously announced INR 1,900 crore investment, and has committed a further INR 900 crore to cold rolling at Hisar and Kharagpur with commissioning planned by Q2 FY28 — together taking CRAP capacity from 2.05 MTPA in FY26 to 2.67 MTPA by FY28 and enabling thinner cold-rolled products. Longer term, a non-binding MoU signed in FY25 with the Government of Maharashtra explores an INR 40,000 crore investment over the next decade for a stainless steel manufacturing facility in the state. On circularity and energy, JSL initiated a new wet milling plant at Jajpur with Harsco Environmental to double slag processing capacity, under a USD 150 million, 15-year agreement; commissioned with AB Energia Solutions Odisha's largest captive industrial solar plant at Jajpur at over 30 MWp (7.324 MWp floating plus 23.02 MWp rooftop, ~44.3 million units a year, cutting CO2 by around 32,208 metric tonnes annually); and partnered Oyster Renewable Energy on a 315.6 MW solar-wind hybrid project in Madhya Pradesh and Gujarat at an investment of INR 132 crore by the Company, expected to abate around 6.5 lakh metric tonnes of carbon a year once fully operational. Its strategic arm Jindal Defense and Aerospace commissioned an electro slag remelting facility for high-performance alloys, and Jindal Stainless Steelway Limited is investing in a dedicated stainless steel fabrication plant after the infrastructure segment grew from a single 2021 project to 20+ executed projects with a pipeline across Indian Railways, state PWDs and municipal corporations. Raw-material backward integration continues through a chrome ore linkage with Odisha Mining Corporation, development of captive mining assets at Sukinda, 70-72% scrap-based inputs, and the 49% stake in the Indonesian NPI joint venture. The Directors' Report technology-absorption list shows a green hydrogen plant and a Zero Liquid Discharge plant imported in 2025-26 and still under commissioning.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Scale and rank — India's largest stainless-steel manufacturer and among the top three stainless-steel producers globally as per SMR (BRSR Section A, types of customers)
- Integrated melting-to-downstream platform: melting, hot rolling, annealing and pickling, cold rolling, long products and specialised downstream solutions, with 4.2 MTPA total melting capacity including 3.0 MTPA in India after the Indonesian melt shop commissioning
- Raw-material security via the Indonesian NPI facility and a melt shop sited close to the nickel source, complemented by in-house ferro-alloy capacity
- Product breadth and R&D — a multi-year R&D roadmap and a dedicated Special Products Division whose FY26 dispatches were the highest ever, supporting a shift to high-value and niche grades
- Certification depth across aerospace, automotive, marine, pressure-equipment, oil & gas and European construction standards, which the Company states widens its addressable market in high-value global segments
- Customer diversification across B2B OEMs, MSMEs (B2ECA), retail (B2C) and government (B2G), spanning 25 Indian states and 41 countries
- Digitalisation — Smart Factory 4.0, an AI Centre of Excellence with an enterprise data platform integrating SAP, manufacturing systems, plant sensors and planning tools, and over 50 identified AI use cases
- Balance-sheet strength cited by management: net debt of INR 3,040 crore, net debt-to-equity of 0.15x and net debt-to-EBITDA of 0.55x entering FY27
